subject: hedgehog
reasoning:
I'm planning the hedgehog model's proportions and coloring using the SDK—roughly 20-25cm long and 10-12cm tall, with a brown/cream body, banded spines, dark snout, and small eyes to keep it stylized but recognizable.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: a root hips joint and a spine chain running from rump to shoulders to neck and head, defining the oval body shape with rounded rump tapering toward the shoulders, all positioned so the feet sit at ground level.

I'm reconsidering the head joint setup — maybe simpler to attach a head joint directly to the spine's last joint with an aim direction angled forward and slightly down, rather than building a separate neck chain. For the actual mesh, I'm leaning toward using a loft to shape the tapering snout, skinned to the joint chain, and thinking through whether the body and head should be one continuous loft or separate pieces.

I'm defining loft stations running from rump to snout tip, each with a width and height, so the body smoothly tapers from a wide chest down through the neck into a pointed nose, with the spines sitting on top of this base shape. I'm still working out how the loft's caps and bone-skinning options behave at the ends.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up a spine chain plus a head joint to drive the loft, then figuring out vertical placement — body centre height, leg length from hip through knee and ankle down to the foot — so the whole hedgehog ends up at a plausible, slightly stylized height once the spines are added on top.

So three points per leg gives hip, knee, and ankle tip joints. For feet, I'm thinking small capsules or spheres attached at the ankle to represent toes, keeping it simple with just a few tiny toe shapes rather than full digit detail to avoid API complexity issues.

I need to double-check the exact function signatures for joint, chain, sweep, and loft before using them, since getting parameters wrong would break the build — things like how bones are passed to skin a mesh, what options loft and sweep accept, and how stations are structured.

Then I continue listing out the remaining builder methods I'll need: part, stick, spike, capsule, rod, along, ring, surface, decal, cards, and extrude, noting their parameter shapes so I can reference them correctly later.

Noting the SDK imports needed from "agentic-3js-builder" plus THREE itself, and the required module exports — meta with name/description and a default build function. I'm also starting to think through a hedgehog's color palette, with cream/tan spines banded with dark brown.

Now I'm planning out the spine geometry: scattering thousands of short cone-like spikes across the back and sides using the body's surface, keeping them off the face and belly, and figuring out how `b.spike` takes a base point and either a direction or tip point to orient each one along the surface normal.

I'm also working out part and triangle budgets—roughly 350 spine parts plus 80 for everything else keeps the total comfortably under the 1000-part limit, with the triangle count manageable too. For coloring, I'm planning to paint each spike with banding along its length using the sweep parameter so the spines read as pale-tipped with a darker band, mimicking real hedgehog spine patterning.

Then I'm estimating texel density across the painted surface area—combining the small spine surfaces and the larger body surface—to figure out roughly how many millimeters per texel I'll get, and whether the banding pattern will still look crisp at that resolution or need a larger paint size.

Weighing whether to bump the paint sheet to 2048 for finer spine banding versus sticking with the default 1024 to avoid atlas overflow issues, since paint resolves through the same part-painting mechanism as other sweeps and lofts. I'm also considering whether banded colors via sector splits would be simpler than paint sweeps, but that adds extra mesh parts, so paint seems cleaner—just need to check segment/side counts for the spike geometry itself.

For the spine shape, I'm leaning toward a low-poly cone using a 5 or 6-sided section rather than the smooth default, giving the spikes a faceted hedgehog-quill look. Each spine needs its tip sharp and base attached to a surface hit point so it inherits the correct bone for skinning, which means passing a direction vector rather than a raw coordinate so the geometry stays correctly weighted to the body.

Now I need to scatter the spines across the body surface, filtering out the face and belly regions so spines only appear on the back, sides, and top of the head — hedgehogs don't have spines on their snouts or undersides. I'm working out the normal-vector and z-coordinate thresholds to exclude those areas while picking a reasonable scatter count like 400 points.

Since individual spine meshes would blow past the part budget if each is separate, I'm thinking about merging many small spine copies into a single combined geometry per paint color, since they share the same bone and coloring anyway — this keeps the part count manageable while still looking dense and realistic.

Since the uv direction is ambiguous either way, I decide it's simpler to just use individual spike parts where s[0] tracks position along each spike directly — 400 parts is well within the 1000 budget and render cost is negligible. For coloring, I'm thinking of hedgehog spines as cream at the base and tip with a dark brown band in the middle, mimicking the natural banded look, so I'll paint based on position along the spike: cream near root, dark band, then cream again toward the tip.

Settling on four bands per spine — dark brown base, cream band, dark brown band, cream tip — each roughly 0.9cm wide on a 3cm spine, which should render crisply enough at 2048 texture resolution. I'm also noting that the spike's tip cap correctly reads t=1 so it picks up the cream tip color, and that the body surface beneath the spines (visible in gaps) should use a countershading paint with dark brown on the back blending to cream on the belly.

For the body paint itself, I'm deciding to use a hard-edged conditional based on surface normal and position (normal pointing down or z past a threshold gets cream, otherwise brown) rather than a mix-based smooth transition, since it's unclear whether the mix helper blends colors or paints reliably — simpler conditionals are safer and the spines will hide most of the body anyway.

Now I'm thinking through the mottled fur texture, nesting a mottle paint as the fallback branch inside a conditional paint function so the back gets subtle brown variation while the belly and face regions still get solid cream, following the pattern where a paint function can return another paint. I also need to work out the face details — dark nose, dark eyes, and a pale muzzle region — to match the classic cartoon hedgehog look.

I'm figuring out the scatter filter conditions for where spines appear versus bare skin: spines on the top and sides of the head and body but excluding the belly and face regions, using normal and position thresholds to carve out those boundaries cleanly around the legs and rump.

Beyond the basic shapes, I'm now brainstorming the small details that add charm — a black nose, eyes with tiny white highlight dots, lathe-shaped ears, small claws on the feet, and a stubby tail, plus wondering whether a few whisker hairs or a tiny grass accent would push the design over the top.

I decide to keep it simple: just the hedgehog alone, no pedestal or props, matching the plain pitch. Now I'm nailing down the actual proportions — nose tip, rump position, overall body length around 0.25-0.3 meters, back height, and foot placement at ground level — leaning toward a chunkier, stylized build rather than strict realism.

I'm working out the leg geometry: short, stubby limbs with two segments each, checking that hip-to-foot distances stay within the limb's reachable range so the knees bend naturally forward when placing the feet.

Front legs get the elbow bulging backward, hind legs the knee bulging forward, giving a rodent-like stance. For the feet themselves, I'm sketching small sole-like shapes resting on the floor, using scaled sphere geometry attached to the end bone of each limb.

I'll build each foot as a capsule running from the ankle joint to a toe point slightly forward and low, letting the bone inheritance pick up naturally at the tip joint, with plans to add small toe bumps afterward.

For leg placement, I'm mapping out where the front and hind leg chains attach to the body: front hips near the shoulders at roughly z≈0.04, x≈±0.045, and hind hips further back near z≈-0.06, x≈±0.05, keeping the leg role consistent so the tip joint reads as the foot.

I'm settling on joint naming conventions for the front and hind leg chains, like shoulderFL/elbowFL/pawFL for the front and hipHL/kneeHL/ankleHL for the back, so each chain's three joints read clearly left-to-right.

I realize the limb function returns points matching lengths.length+1, so a 3-name chain gives two joints plus a tip at the end point. I'm now thinking through passing the limb's point array as a polyline path into the chain builder, since that preserves exact joint positions better than a curve.

For parenting, I need the leg chain to attach to a joint on the spine near the shoulder — likely referencing a specific spine joint index rather than a named lookup. Now I'm sketching out the spine itself: a root "hips" joint with a spine role, positioned near the pelvis, from which the spine chain extends upward.

Working through whether the root joint should have an aim vector or stay unaimed (keeping its bone pointing up) while children orient along the spine curve — I'll leave it unaimed for simplicity. Now I'm plotting catmull-rom points for the spine chain running from the hips to the base of the neck, naming segments spine1, spine2, spine3 as they curve upward and forward.

I'm then placing the neck joint at the chain's final control point and the head joint as its child, tilting the head bone's aim slightly downward and forward so it looks natural, with the head joint sitting outside the main loft but still deforming the mesh through the skinned chain.

I'm also considering whether the mouth needs its own skeleton piece. Since creatures require a separate upper and lower jaw so the mouth can open, I should add a small jaw joint as a child of the head to support that motion.

The upper head loft would taper to the nose tip, while the lower jaw becomes a separate tapered capsule beneath the snout, joined at a hinge point so it can later animate opening and closing.

Now I'm defining the body loft stations themselves, plotting a Catmull curve of width/height values running from the rounded rump through the widest part of the body, narrowing at the shoulders and neck, up toward the head base.

Checking the proportions: head top sits around 0.137 against spine tops near 0.16, and belly bottom near 0.02 leaves enough leg length showing above the ground at 0.012. The muzzle comes out tiny and pointed, which fits a hedgehog's small snout, and the nose tip gets its own black sphere at the end.

Now I'm placing the head joint near the neck/head transition station, aiming it forward toward the nose, and considering whether the spine chain's path should line up closely with the loft's own centerline so the skinning stays consistent.

I'm reworking the spine as a catmull-rom curve through five knots from rump to neck, assigning joint names to each span start so there's no trailing tip joint, then adding a child head joint at the final knot that aims forward-down. I'm also reconsidering whether the root hips joint should sit at the first spine knot or slightly behind it to avoid overlapping positions.

Rethinking the hips placement at the rump with a short bone to spine1, to avoid a zero-length bone where the chain's first joint coincides with the root. I'm deciding to keep hips as a distinct root point and let the spine chain begin slightly offset from it rather than exactly overlapping.

For the limbs, I'm working out which joint should parent each leg (hips for rear legs, spine2 for front legs), and sweeping each limb chain with tapering radii so legs look stubbier at the ankle. I'm placing feet as flattened spheres at the ankle tip with slight ground sink, and adding small toe spheres in front for detail.

For the eyes, I'm placing black bead spheres on the head's surface near the sides using a surface-nearest hit with an embed offset so they protrude naturally, then adding a tiny white highlight sphere offset along the normal and a bit upward to catch light convincingly.

I'm sizing and placing the nose as a flattened black sphere stuck to the snout tip, oriented so it's wide and flat facing forward, and considering a thin mouth line but likely skipping it for simplicity.

For ears, I'm positioning them as flattened ellipsoids stuck to the sides of the head near the back, working out the embed and scale math so they protrude a believable amount, and adding a smaller pink inner-ear disc slightly raised above the ear surface for contrast, accepting some visual approximation in the floating-disc look.

Now I'm setting up the spine scatter logic -- defining a surface sampler over the body with a target count, random seed, minimum spacing, and a filter function based on each hit's normal direction and z-position to exclude certain areas like the face and belly from getting spines.

I'm reasoning through how to pull the normal vector off each scatter hit safely, deciding to treat it as a Vector3-like object with x/y/z properties, then blending it with a backward lean vector to get spine growth directions that angle outward and backward like a real hedgehog's coat.

I'm defining the spike generation per scatter point with randomized length and radius, picking colors and sweep side-counts for a slightly faceted spine look.

Now I'm designing the color palette -- brown for the back coat, dark and cream tones for banding, black for nose and eyes, pink for ears and feet -- and writing a paint function that switches between a mottled brown texture and cream based on position (forelimb z-coordinate and underside normal) to carve out a pale belly and face against a brown back.

I'm deciding to skip whiskers and a tail stub to keep the rig simpler, and sketching out a jaw joint and lower jaw capsule under the snout, checking the geometry so the chin pokes out just slightly below the snout's loft profile instead of being fully hidden inside it.

Now I'm laying out the leg root and target joints for all four limbs, mirroring left and right using a sign multiplier on the x-coordinate for shoulder and hip placement.

I'm computing root-to-target distances for front and hind legs against their segment lengths to confirm they're reachable, choosing bend directions (elbow back, knee forward) and setting target positions so the feet land just outside the body's belly width at each station.
